title: Getting CRA Compliant Hardens the Code and Gets Your Company Closer to Digital Sovereignty
gist: OpenSSF's Christopher 'CRob' Robinson explains how Scorecard, the 41-control Security Baseline (mapped to EU CRA and NIST SSDF) and SLSA harden open-source supply chains. He expects CRA-aligned laws to spread before full CRA enforcement on December 11, 2027, argues AI coding needs security harnesses (OpenSSF's Cyber Reasoning System), and calls open source the foundation of digital sovereignty.

insights.claim: OpenSSF's Security Baseline distills regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act and the NIST Secure Software Development Framework into 41 recommended, verifiable security controls for open-source maintainers and consumers, mixing technical settings like branch protection with organizational controls like a published security policy.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Expect Security Baseline conformance to become a procurement signal for open-source dependencies used by CRA-bound manufacturers.
insights.locator: First, I would highlight our Security Baseline

insights.claim: Level 1 of OpenSSF's three-level Security Baseline roughly equals a mid-range Scorecard score, focuses mainly on documentation, and takes an experienced developer about two hours to implement.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Low adoption cost suggests fast uptake among maintainers seeking downstream enterprise users.
insights.locator: The Security Baseline is structured across three maturity levels

insights.claim: OpenSSF Scorecard serves both as a tool for choosing dependencies and as a public signal of a project's security rigor, letting enterprises such as banks, hospitals and retailers pick the package with the stronger security posture.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Security posture scores may increasingly drive open-source dependency selection and thus project adoption.

insights.claim: SLSA complements Scorecard and Security Baseline by hardening the underlying build infrastructure — IDEs, developer workstations, source repositories, CI/CD pipelines and distribution — across progressive maturity levels for provenance and integrity.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Build-provenance tooling is a durable spend area as supply-chain attacks rise.
insights.locator: The second framework I recommend is SLSA

insights.claim: Sonatype reports show a decline in open-source project maintenance since the pandemic, which opens doors for supply-chain attack vectors such as typosquatting and version manipulation seen in the Python ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Under-maintained dependencies are a growing attack surface, supporting demand for supply-chain security vendors.
insights.locator: For instance, Sonatype reports showed a decline

insights.claim: The EU Cyber Resilience Act exempts open-source maintainers who do not profit from their work, but commercial consumers integrating that software must comply, pushing compliance demands upstream indirectly.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Manufacturers selling into the EU carry CRA liability for open-source components, driving demand for SBOM and component-assurance tooling.
insights.locator: The EU CRA explicitly exempts open-source maintainers

insights.claim: The UK, India, Japan and Australia are watching the EU CRA rollout ahead of its full enforcement date of December 11, 2027, and Robinson expects other regions to introduce CRA-aligned legislation in coming years.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: CRA-style rules could become a global standard, expanding the addressable market for software supply-chain compliance tools.
insights.locator: Global jurisdictions are watching the EU CRA closely

insights.claim: Fragmented cybersecurity regulations across regions, such as one adopting standard SBOM formats while another mandates a proprietary 86-point list, would create conflicting compliance burdens that slow software delivery.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Harmonization vs fragmentation of CRA-like rules is a key variable for compliance costs of global software vendors.
insights.locator: Fragmented rules would create significant friction

insights.claim: LLM coding tools are bringing non-developers in accounting, marketing and operations into code creation, and in the rush to adopt them teams risk bypassing 50 years of established software engineering and security discipline unless guardrails are built in.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Rising volume of AI-generated code from non-engineers increases demand for automated security guardrails in AI coding harnesses.
insights.quote: teams risk overlooking 50 years of established software engineering discipline and security practices
insights.locator: In the rush to adopt AI capabilities

insights.claim: OpenSSF hired a dedicated AI Security Architect to deploy its Open Source Software Cyber Reasoning System, a modular harness for plugging in AI models with security skills, and plans to release Scorecard, SLSA and Security Insights skills next year so agents enforce security practices during code generation.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Security 'skills' for coding agents are an emerging layer; watch open-source standards shaping agent harnesses.
insights.locator: That has been OpenSSF's main focus this year

insights.claim: Robinson describes himself as an AI realist: LLMs perform statistical prediction rather than reasoning and can be wrong, their strength is pattern-finding over vast data, and using them without security understanding risks leaking sensitive personal or corporate data to external models.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Data-leakage risk to external models remains a governance concern, supporting private/local model deployment.
insights.locator: I consider myself an AI realist

insights.claim: Open-source AI contribution policies vary: the Linux kernel permits AI-assisted contributions under developer review while smaller projects with fewer review resources may restrict them, and Robinson's priority is that every project publish an explicit AI contribution policy.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Maintainer capacity, strained by AI-generated reports and PRs, is a bottleneck for open-source security.
insights.locator: Policies cross open source remain varied

insights.claim: Open-source software is the most reliable foundation for digital sovereignty because organizations can inspect, fork and modify code and combine best-of-breed components, such as an open-weight LLM on European cloud hosting, without vendor lock-in.
insights.speaker: Christopher Robinson
insights.so_what: Sovereignty concerns favor open-source and open-weight stacks and European cloud hosting over single-vendor platforms.
insights.quote: open-source software provides the most reliable foundation for organizations to maintain autonomy and avoid vendor lock-in
insights.locator: To tie this back to digital sovereignty

insights.claim: Local-first software architecture, where users retain control of their data locally rather than relying on centralized cloud providers, complements European user-rights regulation as a path to data ownership.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Local-first architectures may gain traction in regulated European markets.
insights.locator: This aligns with the local-first software movement
